The story of the lighthouse, as it continues, finds itself woven into the fabric of a larger, quieter landscape. The tower, once a solitary sentinel against the sky, becomes a reference point in the minds of those who have spent their lives along the shore. The memory of its light fades, replaced by the memory of the water itself. The tide is no longer a warning, but a rhythm that marks the passage of time. It is a rhythm that can be felt on the sand, a gentle pull that reminds us of our own small place in the vastness.

The keeper's cottage, though no longer inhabited, remains a testament to the hands that once built it. The grey stone, the slate roof, the deep windows — these are the elements of the land that have been preserved. The tin of tea, left on the shelf, has long since been forgotten, but the memory of it lingers in the air. It is a small, personal detail that connects us to the past. The act of remembering these things is a form of care, a way of ensuring that the landscape does not become just a map, but a place we can still feel.
